AK.note: Most of Alaska closes at midnight ET; the Aleutians west of Umnak at 1 a.m.

FL-special.note: Peninsula and most of the state at 7; the Central-time Panhandle counties at 8.

ID.note: Mountain-time Idaho at 10; the Pacific-time north at 11.

KS.note: All but four Mountain-time counties close at 8.

KY.note: Eastern-time Kentucky at 6; the Central-time west at 7.

MI.note: All but four Upper Peninsula counties close at 8.

NE.note: 8 p.m. Central and 7 p.m. Mountain, so the whole state closes at once.

OR.note: Vote by mail; Malheur County (Mountain time) at 10, the rest at 11.

SD.note: Central-time east at 8; the Mountain-time west at 9.

TX.note: All but El Paso and Hudspeth counties close at 8.

GA.note: A candidate needs a majority of the vote to win outright; otherwise the top two meet in a runoff on Dec. 1, 2026.

ME.note: Maine uses ranked-choice voting for the Senate race. If nobody wins a majority of first choices, the ballots go to Augusta for a centralized count; the upload and verification has taken a week to ten days, so a close race may not be settled until mid-November.

AK.note: Only first-choice results are reported on election night and through the absentee window; the Division of Elections runs the ranked-choice tabulation on Nov. 18. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day count if received within 10 days (15 from abroad).

NC.note: Mail ballots must be in by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day, with no postmark grace period (a 2023 law ended it). Mail and early-vote results post between 7:30 and 9:30 p.m., precincts by about midnight; only provisional, cured and military/overseas ballots are added later.

MI.note: Clerks in jurisdictions over 5,000 people may pre-process absentee ballots for up to eight days before Election Day (smaller ones the Monday before), with no totals released before 8 p.m.; first used in 2024, it makes absentee reporting much faster than in 2020.

NE.note: Early ballots must reach county officials by the close of polls.

NH.note: Towns set their own hours (open by 11 a.m., closed no earlier than 7 p.m.); in practice they close at 7 or 8 p.m. Ballots are counted locally, by machine in most towns and by hand in more than 120 small ones.

TX.note: Most counties post early-voting and mail totals right after polls close locally; Bexar County (San Antonio) says it will hold its early results until lines clear.

FL.note: State law requires early-voting and mail results within 30 minutes of poll closing and precinct updates at least every 45 minutes, so Florida counts fast.

OH.note: Under Senate Bill 293 (signed Dec. 2025, first used in the May 2026 primary) mail ballots must be received by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day regardless of postmark; the old four-day grace period is gone.

IA.note: Absentee ballots must reach the county auditor by 8 p.m. Central on Election Day.

KS.note: Counties may keep polls open until 8 p.m. local, and the Mountain-time counties until 7 p.m. Mountain (9 p.m. ET). Counties vary in how they release results.

MN.note: Mail ballots must be received by 8 p.m. Central. First results usually appear around 8:30 p.m. Central, with complete unofficial results early Wednesday.

ALL.note: The AP will not declare a winner before the final poll-closing time in a state. It calls noncompetitive races at poll close from its VoteCast survey and voting history, and competitive ones only once enough votes are counted to make the winner clear.
